text: Socrates builds his city out of need rather than from an idea: “none of us is self-sufficient” (Republic II.369b). The first citizens are a farmer, a builder, a weaver, and a shoemaker, each doing the one work for which his nature fits him (369d–370c). If the city remained at that size, it would need no soldier. Glaucon will not live in it. He wants couches and side dishes, and Socrates grants the demand by admitting the luxurious, “feverish” city (372e). Once appetite grows in that way, war follows, because the land that fed the healthy city will not feed the feverish one. The feverish city must take land from its neighbors and defend its own (373d–e). A class of warriors therefore becomes necessary, and the rest of the reading turns on the question of what kind of person can be trusted with weapons. Socrates finds his model in the well-bred dog, gentle to those it knows and fierce to strangers (375a–e). From the dog comes the first of the city’s many surprises: since the guardian distinguishes friend from enemy by knowledge, the guardian is already a philosopher of a kind (376b–c).
